Arthur Finch had the peculiar sensation that a gear had skipped a tooth somewhere in the world. He was an horologist; his world was one of cogs and escapements, of the steady, civilized parcelling of eternity. But the grand regulator on his workbench, a masterpiece of brass and steel, had just chimed thirteen. He stared at it. That was not possible. He tapped the bell with a fingernail; it gave a clean, honest ring. He looked about the workshop, at the hundred faces of his clocks, all ticking in a reassuring chorus. Then he heard a floorboard creak by the window, a sound entirely out of time with the room’s metronomic pulse. All men, however dedicated to mechanics, carry a vestige of ghost-lore within them. A profound wrongness settled in his stomach. He secured the door to the street, came back to his bench, and set down his loupe. Suddenly, with a jolt, he perceived a coat, a heavy tweed thing he did not own, hanging in the air between him and the window. He blinked. It was an empty coat, shoulders slumped as if on a hanger, but there was no hanger. He would have dismissed it as a waking dream, but a tremor ran through the fabric, and a voice spoke, seeming to come from the very collar of the thing.

“Finch!” said the Voice.

“Eh?” said Finch, his jaw slack.

“Don’t lose your head,” said the Voice. “I’m a bit out of sorts.”

Finch made no reply for a moment, simply gaping at the coat. “Out of sorts,” he repeated dumbly.

“That’s one way of putting it,” replied the Voice. The story from the morning paper, of a man who’d vanished from a moving omnibus, flashed through his mind. He did not seem to be particularly terrified, not yet. The shock was too great for fear. Realisation was a slower machine. “I thought that was a hoax,” he said. The thought uppermost in his mind was the sheer mechanical impossibility. “Are you wearing that coat?” he asked.

“Yes,” said the man who was not there.

“Oh!” said Finch, and then shook himself. “I say!” he said. “But this is absurd. It’s some sort of projection.” He stepped forward quickly, his hand reaching for the tweed, and met a shoulder of shocking solidity. He snatched his hand back as if burned, a gasp escaping him.

“Steady, Finch, for God’s sake! I need a place to rest. Stop!” The coat sleeve shot out and a hand gripped his wrist. He cried out.

“Finch!” cried the Voice. “Finch! Settle down!” and the grip became iron. A desperate need to break free seized him. The hand of the tweed-clad arm clamped onto his shoulder, and he was suddenly pulled off balance and thrown against a display case of pocket watches. He opened his mouth to shout, and a dusty corner of the coat was stuffed into it. The Unseen Man had him pinned, but his legs were free and he kicked and thrashed wildly.

“Will you just listen?” said the Unseen Man, holding on despite a sharp kick to the shin. “By God, you’ll have me completely undone in a moment!”

“Lie still, you madman!” roared the Unseen Man in Finch’s ear.

Finch struggled for another second and then went limp.

“If you make a scene, I’ll knock you senseless,” said the Unseen Man, removing the coat from his mouth. “I’m not a ghost. It isn’t magic. It’s a temporal displacement. And I need your help. I don’t want to harm you, but if you carry on like a spooked horse, I must. Don’t you know me, Finch? Elias, from the university club?”

“Let me stand,” said Finch. “I’ll be still. And let me have a moment to think.” He stood up and rubbed his jaw.

“I am Elias Thorne, from the club, and I have become unstuck in time. I am just an ordinary man; a man you know; made unstable.”

“Elias?” said Finch.

“Elias,” answered the Voice. “The fellow who argued with you about relativity, with the wild hair and the spectacles, who always spilled his brandy.”

“I am dizzy,” said Finch. “My thoughts are a riot. What has this to do with Elias?”

“I _am_ Elias.”

Finch thought. “It’s monstrous,” he said. “But what sheer lunacy must occur to make a man unstable?”

“It’s no lunacy. It’s a process, dreadfully logical—”

“It’s monstrous!” said Finch. “How in Heaven’s name—?”

“It’s monstrous enough. But I’m exhausted and fading... Great Scott! Finch, you’re a man of reason. Be calm. Get me some brandy and let me sit down.”

Finch watched as the tweed coat drifted across the room, then saw his own visitor’s chair groan as if under a great weight. It settled, and the leather cushion indented visibly. He rubbed his temples and felt his own pulse. “This is worse than spirits,” he said, and gave a short, choked laugh.

“That’s better. Thank goodness, you’re finding your senses!”

“Or losing them,” said Finch, and squeezed his eyes shut. “Get me some brandy. I feel faint.”

“It didn’t seem so. Where are you? If I move will I disrupt you? _There_! all right. Brandy? Here. Where do I give it to you?”

The chair creaked and Finch felt the decanter lifted from his grasp. He let it go with a supreme effort; his every nerve screamed against it. The decanter came to rest, hovering a foot above the chair’s seat. He stared at it, utterly perplexed. “This is—this must be—a delusion. You have convinced me you are here.”

“Nonsense,” said the Voice. “It’s quite real.”

“Listen to me.”

“I proved conclusively last Tuesday,” began Finch, “that travel through the fourth dimension—”

“Never mind your proofs! I’m fading,” said the Voice, “and the moments are cold when you’re not wearing them properly.”

“Food?” said Finch.

The brandy decanter tilted. “Yes,” said the Unseen Man, setting it down with a rap. “Have you a blanket?”

Finch muttered something under his breath. He went to a small cupboard and produced a woollen travel rug. “This serve?” he asked. It was taken from him. It hung limp for a second, then draped itself, rose and fell with unseen breath, and settled into the chair. “Trousers, a shirt, anything would be a mercy,” said the Unseen, curtly. “And food.”

“Anything. But this is the most irrational event I have ever encountered!” He found a spare shirt and trousers, then went to his small pantry. He returned with a loaf of bread and some cheese, pulled up a small table, and set them before his guest.

“No need for a knife,” said his visitor, and a wedge of cheese levitated, a bite vanishing from it with a faint chewing sound.

“Unstuck!” said Finch, and sat heavily on a stool.

“I always feel better with something solid around me,” said the Unseen Man, with a full mouth, eating with alarming speed. “Odd, I know.”

“I suppose that arm is stable,” said Finch.

“Trust me,” said the Unseen Man.

“Of all the impossible, confounding—”

“Precisely. But it’s a stroke of luck I stumbled into _your_ workshop. My first good fortune! In any case I meant to hide here tonight. You must allow it! It’s a damnable problem, this flickering, isn’t it? Almost came apart completely over there. The coherence fails when I’m tired, you see. It’s only the living matter I’ve affected.... I’ve been in this street for six hours.”

“But how is it done?” began Finch, his voice sharp with frustration. “Confound it! The entire proposition; it’s illogical from start to finish.”

“Quite logical,” said the Unseen Man. “Painfully logical.” He reached out and the brandy decanter was his. Finch stared at the consuming blanket. A beam of light from the streetlamp, passing through a thin patch in the wool, made a strange, shimmering triangle on the floor beneath. “What was that commotion?” he asked. “How did the police chase begin?”

“There was an absolute fool of a physicist; a partner of mine, you might say; who tried to steal my equations. _Has_ stolen them.”

“Is _he_ unstable too?”

“No.”

“Well?”

“Can’t I have more to eat before I explain all that? I’m starving; in pain. And you want a lecture!”

Finch stood. “_You_ didn’t cause that panic in the street?” he asked.

“Not I,” said his visitor. “Some idiot constable saw me flicker and lost his nerve. A whole crowd got hysterical. They were frightened of me. Curse them! I say; I need more to eat than this, Finch.”

“I’ll see what is in the kitchen,” said Finch. “Not much, I expect.”

After he had finished eating, and he ate a great deal, the Unseen Man requested a pipe. He bit the stem so hard it nearly cracked before Finch could offer a light, and cursed when a flicker of his own hand made him drop it. It was bizarre to see him smoke; his lips, jaw, and throat became momentarily visible as a swirling, three dimensional cloud of grey smoke. “This blessed comfort of tobacco!” he said, and puffed greedily. “I am fortunate to have found you, Finch. You must help me. Fancy landing on your doorstep just now! I’m in a hellish mess; I’ve been reckless, I think. The things I have endured! But we will achieve things yet. Let me tell you—” He helped himself to more brandy. Kemp got up, looked around him, and fetched a second glass from a cupboard. “It’s mad; but I suppose I am allowed a drink.”

“You haven’t the foggiest notion,” said Elias, his voice a low growl from the depths of the blanket. “It began in a laboratory, with a spinning coil and a theory. A theory you called nonsense…”

“You haven’t the foggiest notion,” said Elias, his voice a low growl from the depths of the blanket. “It began in a laboratory, with a spinning coil and a theory. A theory you called nonsense…”

Finch stared, the glass halfway to his lips. “I call a great many things nonsense, Elias. It is the foundation of scientific rigour. Which particular nonsense are we discussing?”

“The nonsense of dimensional resonance!” the voice from the blanket snapped, with a sudden ferocity that made Finch start. “The idea that matter is not so solid as we perceive it, but is a vibration, a wave form that can be… altered. Tuned, if you will, to a different frequency of existence. You said it was metaphysics, not physics. You laughed at my paper at the Royal Society.”

The memory, half-buried under years of subsequent papers and experiments, surfaced in Finch’s mind. A younger Elias Thorne, eyes alight with a feverish and, to Finch’s mind, unscientific passion. Arguing for a holistic theory of matter and energy that bordered on the mystical. Finch had dismissed it curtly. “The Thorne Postulate. Good heavens. You pursued that madness?”

“I proved it!” came the triumphant, yet ragged, reply. A swirl of smoke erupted from the vicinity of the blanket’s collar. “I built the resonator. A series of nested magnetic coils, spinning in contra-rotation, generating a field of… well, the mathematics are formidable. But it worked. I stepped into the field, Finch. I tuned the resonance of my own body.”

“To what end?” Finch asked, his voice now a whisper. He sat down again, slowly, as if his legs might not support him. “What did you hope to achieve by… tuning yourself?”

“To pass through solid matter, of course! The ultimate exploration. To walk through walls, to descend through the earth, to be unbound by physical limitation. That was the theory. The practice…” The voice trailed off. The blanket seemed to shudder. “The practice was… imperfect.”

“Imperfect,” Finch repeated, with a dry, hollow laugh. “You call this state of flickering non-existence imperfect? Elias, it’s a catastrophe. You haven’t made yourself able to pass through walls; you have made yourself come undone.”

“I know that now, you fool!” Elias roared, and the brandy decanter on the small table jumped as an unseen hand slammed down beside it. “The resonance is unstable! I can’t hold it. I can’t collapse the field. I am caught between states, like a reflection in two opposing mirrors. And this… this flickering. It’s getting worse. The cohesion fails. It takes all my concentration just to remain in one piece.”

Suddenly, the blanket sagged abruptly, falling inwards as if whatever supported it had vanished. A brief and terrible transparency overcame it; for a single, sickening heartbeat, Finch saw not a man, not even the ghost of a man, but a momentary tracery of glowing blue veins and a branching of nerves, hanging in the air like a diagram in a medical text, shot through with a faint, smoky light. Then, with a sound like tearing fabric, the form reasserted itself and the blanket was once more filled.

Finch recoiled, his knuckles white on the arm of his chair. “God help us,” he breathed.

“He will not. But you will,” said the Unseen Man, his voice strained and weak after the effort. “I saw the lights in your workshop. I know what you work on here. Coherers, accumulators, high-energy capacitors. Your work is more advanced than any in London. You have the equipment. And you have the mind, Finch. For all your damnable skepticism, you have the mind.”

“And what is it you imagine I can do?”

“Help me build a counter-resonator! A larger, more stable one. Something to collapse the field, to ground me, to bring me back. The theory is sound; it is my engineering that was flawed, under-powered. Your workshop… it is my only hope.”

Finch got to his feet and began to pace the cluttered floor of his workshop. He strode between a half-assembled dynamo and a rack of glass vacuum tubes, his mind a maelstrom of impossibilities; his workshop, his sanctuary, had been invaded by a nightmare that claimed to be his former colleague. A nightmare that was now making demands.

“And if I refuse?” he asked, stopping to face the blanket-shrouded chair.

“Then I shall most likely disintegrate,” said the voice, with a chilling lack of emotion. “Perhaps quietly. Perhaps not. The energy contained in my body’s matter, if released at once… it could be quite catastrophic. It might level this entire street. Or, I may simply haunt this place, a flickering, mindless collection of sensations, until the end of time. But before that, I assure you, I will make your life an unbearable misery. I am still a man, Finch, with a man’s strength. You cannot see me, but I can trip you on the stairs. I can hold your head under the water in your basin. I can set your workshop ablaze. Do not test my desperation.”

The cold, matter-of-fact threat was more terrifying than any outburst. Finch felt a chill that had nothing to do with the night air. He was a prisoner in his own home. He looked at the locked door, the bolted windows. They were no defense at all.

“And this… partner?” Finch asked, seizing on a different thread. “The one who stole your equations?”

“Ah, Davies,” Elias spat. The name was a curse. “My assistant. A plodding, unimaginative little man I trusted to check my calculations. He saw the final test. He saw me vanish. And while I was… adjusting… reeling from the sheer horror and triumph of it, he ran. With my notebooks. With all of it.”

“Why?”

“Why do men do anything? For fame! For money! To sell the secret to the highest bidder; the War Office, the Germans, anyone. Or worse, to try it himself! To build his own resonator, to follow me into this hell, but with my notes to guide him past the mistakes. He has the theory, Finch! He just needs the engineering. He is a danger to everyone.”

The narrative was becoming more and more insane, a fever dream of scientific hubris and melodrama. And yet, there sat the proof, a blanket animated by a desperate, disembodied voice. He felt a frantic desire to reject it all, to declare Elias a hallucination and himself mad. But the brandy glass on the table, the one Elias had drunk from, was undeniably empty. The pipe smoke still hung in the air, a visible remnant of an invisible act.

“I need your schematics,” said Elias, his voice urgent, pulling Finch from his reverie. “Your designs for the new magnetic drivers. And access to your power supply. We must begin at once. Time is… it is a very real, very finite quantity for me now.”

Feinch ran a hand through his hair. “This is preposterous. To build such a device would take weeks, months! It would require materials I do not have. Specialized castings, refined conductors…”

“We will make do!” the voice insisted. “We will cannibalise what you have. My mind and your hands, Finch! It is the only way. Now, clear that main workbench. We have work to do.”

Finch stood motionless, his mind refusing to accept the command. He was a man of order, of quiet contemplation and methodical work. This… this was chaos. This was a madman in a blanket ordering him to dismantle his life’s work on the strength of an impossible story.

And then a new sound intruded.

It was faint at first, but clear in the relative silence of the workshop. The sound of heavy, rhythmic footsteps on the cobblestones outside. More than one set. They stopped directly in front of the building.

Elias fell silent. The blanket became utterly still. Finch found he was holding his breath.

A sharp, authoritative knock hammered on the workshop door.

“Mr. Finch!” a voice called from the street. A voice used to being obeyed. “Open up! This is Inspector Davies of Scotland Yard.”

Finch’s blood ran cold. Davies. The name Elias had just spat like a venomous dart. It could not be a coincidence.

“Don’t answer,” hissed the voice from the chair, a mere thread of sound. “Don’t even breathe.”

The knocking came again, louder this time. “Mr. Finch, I have a warrant to search these premises! Open this door at once, or we shall force it!”

Finch looked from the door to the chair in a panic. An Inspector Davies. Here. Now. It was too much. His mind, accustomed to the slow, stately progress of logic and evidence, was breaking under the strain of these frantic, cascading events. He felt a surge of anger at Elias. This was his fault. This circus of policemen and stolen secrets had followed him here, to this quiet sanctuary.

“What do I do?” Finch mouthed silently at the blanket.

The unseen head seemed to turn towards the door. “He knows I’m here. Or he suspects. He must have tracked me. The fool. He’s brought the police into it.” The voice was a low, dangerous murmur. “You must get rid of him. Tell him anything. Tell him you’ve been working late, you heard nothing.”

“And if he insists on coming in?” Finch whispered, his throat dry.

“You will not let him,” the voice commanded, and a cold spot moved past Finch as Elias apparently rose from the chair. Finch felt a light pressure on his arm, the unmistakable grip of invisible fingers. It was not a comforting touch; it was a manacle. “You are a respectable man, Finch. A man of science. Your word carries weight. Use it. Lie to him. For if he enters this room, I will be forced to take measures. And they will not be pleasant. For any of us.”

The threat hung in the air, more potent than the smell of ozone from Finch’s dynamos. Finch, a man who had dedicated his life to the pursuit of truth, was being commanded to lie by a creature born of a lie. The irony was not lost on him, even in his terror.

“Mr. Finch! I will ask you one last time!”

He had no choice. He was trapped between an invisible madman and the Metropolitan Police. Taking a shaky breath, Finch walked towards the door, the invisible pressure on his arm guiding him, reminding him who was truly in command.

“One moment, Inspector!” Finch called out, trying to keep his voice steady. He fumbled with the heavy bolts, his hands shaking. This was it. He was choosing. He was becoming an accomplice. He drew the last bolt and pulled the heavy wooden door inward just a crack.

A portly man in a heavy coat and a bowler hat stood on his doorstep, flanked by two uniformed constables. The man’s face was florid and impatient, and he held a piece of paper in his hand. “Dr. Alistair Finch?” he demanded.

“I am Finch,” he said, blocking the doorway with his body. “What is the meaning of this intrusion, Inspector? It is the middle of the night.”

“Inspector Davies, as I said,” the man grunted, flashing a warrant. “We are in pursuit of a fugitive, Doctor. A dangerous man. We have reason to believe he may have sought shelter in this street. We are searching all properties.”

Finch’s heart hammered against his ribs. “A fugitive? Here? That’s absurd. This is a quiet street. I have been in my workshop since dusk and have seen or heard nothing untoward.”

Inspector Davies’s eyes narrowed. He peered past Finch, trying to get a look into the shadowy depths of the workshop. “My information is quite specific, Doctor. We are looking for a man named Elias Thorne. A former associate of yours, I believe?”

The directness of the question struck Finch like a physical blow. This was not a random search. This was targeted. “Elias Thorne?” Finch said, feigning a mild, academic surprise. “Good heavens, I haven’t seen Thorne in years. Not since he was laughed out of the Royal Society. What has he done?”

“He is wanted for questioning in connection with a violent disturbance in Bloomsbury, and for the theft of sensitive scientific materials,” Davies said sharply, his gaze unwavering. “He was seen fleeing in this direction. He is described as being… unwell. Unstable. Have you truly seen nothing, Doctor?”

A.

Every shadow seemed to hold a threat, every creak of the floorboards sounded like a footstep behind him. He found a joint of cold beef, a loaf of bread, some cheese. He worked mechanically, his mind a turmoil of frantic, useless thoughts. He was a scientist. He had to think his way out. But how? How to fight a man who was everywhere and nowhere? A man who held his life, and Adye’s, on a whim? He carried the laden tray back up the stairs. As he entered the drawing room, he saw the scarlet dressing gown standing by the window, peering out into the moonlit garden. “A quiet night,” the Voice commented, without turning. “The world sleeps, ignorant of the power that has been born into it. They will learn, Kemp. They will all learn.” The dressing gown turned, and the empty sleeves gestured towards the table. “Put it there. Good. You are an excellent servant, Kemp. Perhaps there is a place for you in the new world after all.” The gnawing sounds began again, loud and bestial in the quiet room. Kemp sat down in another chair, as far from the ghastly spectacle as he could manage. He watched, fascinated and repulsed, as chunks of beef vanished in mid-air and the level of the whiskey in the bottle lowered once more. He had to keep him talking. That was the only thing he could think of. A man who was talking was not, for the moment, killing. And a man who was talking might reveal a weakness. “Your notes,” Kemp began, his voice carefully modulated to sound inquisitive, not challenging. “What is in them that is so important? Surely the process is in your head.” Griffin paused in his eating. “The process, yes. The broad strokes of it. But the details, Kemp! The intricate formulae, the precise refractive indices, the notes on pigmentation and tissue density. It is not one formula, but thousands. A cascade of treatments. To reverse the process, to become visible again… that is a problem I have not yet solved. The notes contain my preliminary thoughts. My theories. Without them, I am trapped like this forever.” A flicker of something new ignited in Kemp’s mind. Hope? No, it was too fragile a thing to be called hope. It was merely a possibility. A long shot. Reversing the process. If Griffin could be made visible again, he would be just a man. A very large, strong, and homicidal man, but a man nonetheless. A man who could be caught, who could be stopped. “So you want to become visible again?” Kemp asked. “Of course I do!” the Voice snapped, with a sudden return to its earlier irritability. “Do you think this is a pleasure? To be a phantom? To be naked in the cold? To be unable to eat or drink in public? It is a cursed existence! I will be visible when I choose to be. When it suits my purpose. I will be master of my own state, Kemp. Visible one moment, invisible the next. That is true power. But to get there, I need my books.” “And you’re certain you can do it? Reverse it?” “The principle is there,” Griffin said, more calmly. He reached for the whiskey bottle again. The neck of the bottle tilted, and a long glug of liquor poured into the unseen glass. “It is a matter of reversing the blood decolorization without coagulating it. A delicate operation. It might require a second party to administer the final stages. A trusted assistant.” He paused, and the implication hung in the air between them, thick and cloying. “You see our futures are intertwined, Kemp. I need you. For now.” Kemp’s mind raced. This was it. This was the key. He had to get those books. Not for Griffin, but for himself. If the secret to reversing the process was in those notes, then they were the most important things in the world. They were his only weapon. He had to play along. He had to become the most loyal, the most eager, the most indispensable confederate Griffin could ever wish for. He had to win his trust completely. It was a perilous game, a dance on a razor’s edge. “I see,” Kemp said slowly, letting a note of dawning comprehension, of reluctant ambition, enter his voice. “I begin to see. It is… an extraordinary vision.” “Vision?” scoffed the Invisible Man. “It is not a vision, it is a timetable. It is practical physics. Now, to the matter of Iping. We need a plan. The town will be watched. The police will be everywhere.” He fell silent for a moment, the only sound the faint clink of the glass being set down on the table. “You will need a story. A good one. A sick relative, perhaps. An urgent summons. Something to explain a sudden journey at night. You must be convincing.” Suddenly, a new sound intruded. Sharp, rhythmic, and clear in the night’s silence. It was a knocking. Not at the main door this time, but at the smaller side door, the one that led from the garden into Kemp’s laboratory. It was a firm, official-sounding knock. Kemp froze, his blood turning to ice. The dressing gown became rigid. “Stay here,” the Voice commanded, a mere whisper of sound. “Do not move a muscle.” Kemp heard the faint creak of the chair, and then nothing. The absolute silence of the Invisible Man’s movement was more terrifying than any footstep. The knocking came again, louder this time. “Dr. Kemp? Are you in there? It’s Constable Adkins, sir. We saw a light.” Kemp’s heart hammered against his ribs. He sat paralysed, staring at the door of the drawing room, expecting it to open, expecting to be told what to do. But no command came. The Invisible Man was gone. Had he abandoned him? Was this a test? The knocking was insistent now. “Dr. Kemp! Is everything alright, sir?” He had to answer. Silence would be an admission that something was wrong. With a supreme effort of will, he pushed himself to his feet. His legs felt like lead. He walked to the drawing room door and into the hall. He could feel the constable’s presence on the other side of the laboratory door, a symbol of the normal, lawful world he was now forever barred from. He took a deep, shuddering breath. “One moment, Constable,” he called out, his voice sounding thin and reedy to his own ears. “I am coming.” He walked through the hall, past the foot of the stairs where Adye lay bound and helpless, and into his laboratory. The room was dark, save for the moonlight slanting through the tall windows. His hand was on the bolt of the side door when he felt it. A sudden, intense coldness beside him. And then the whisper, so close it was like a thought in his own brain. “Let him in, Kemp. Be normal. I will be here. Listening.” The barrel of the revolver pressed, cold and hard, into the small of his back. Kemp’s last sliver of self-possession shattered. He was not being tested. He was being used as a human shield. He fumbled with the bolt, his fingers clumsy and numb. He pulled the door open. Constable Adkins stood on the threshold, his helmet in his hand, his face ruddy and concerned in the moonlight. “Dr. Kemp, sir. Sorry to disturb you so late. The Inspector was worried. With all the goings on, and Colonel Adye not reporting back… we saw your lights on and thought we’d best check.” “The Colonel?” Kemp said, struggling to keep his teeth from chattering. “He… he left some time ago. He was following a lead.” It was a feeble lie, but it was the best he could manage. The pressure of the gun in his back was an unanswerable argument against any other course of action. “Oh, did he now?” the constable said, peering past Kemp into the darkened lab. “Funny, his man is still waiting with the carriage down the road. Said the Colonel told him to wait, no matter what.” Kemp’s mind went blank with panic. He could offer no explanation. He just stared at the constable, his face a pale mask of terror. “Are you quite well, sir?” Adkins asked, his brow furrowed with genuine concern. “You look as if you’ve seen a ghost.” “I am… I am overwrought,” Kemp stammered. “The events of the day… this business with the Invisible Man… it is unsettling.” Behind him, he felt the gun press harder. A silent command. End this. Get rid of him. “Of course, sir. Understandable,” the constable said, though his eyes were still full of doubt. “Well, as long as you’re safe. The Inspector just wanted to be sure. We’re setting up a cordon around the town. No one in or out without being checked. If you see or hear anything, sir, anything at all…” “I will, Constable. Of course. Thank you for your concern. Good night.” Kemp began to close the door. The constable, however, put a hand out to stop it. “Just one more thing, sir. We found this at the bottom of your drive, near the gate.” He held up his other hand. In it dangled a small, dark object. A man’s glove. A thick, woollen driving glove. It was Adye’s. Kemp must have knocked it from the Colonel’s pocket during the struggle. “Thought it might be yours, sir,” the constable said, holding it out. Kemp stared at the glove as if it were a venomous snake. He could not take it. He could not touch it. “No,” he said, his voice a strained whisper. “No, it is not mine.” “Ah. Well then. Good night, sir.” The constable nodded, pocketed the glove, and finally let the door close. Kemp shot the bolt and leaned against the door, his body trembling violently. He had survived. For a few more moments, he had survived. The pressure in his back was gone. “You see?” the Voice said, from the centre of the room. It was conversational, almost light. “It is not so difficult. You are a natural actor, Kemp.” Kemp did not answer. He was listening to the constable’s retreating footsteps crunching on the gravel path. Each step was taking him further away from safety, from sanity, from the world of men. Each step was leaving him alone again. Alone with the Invisible Man. “That was a mistake, however,” Griffin continued, and the light tone was gone, replaced by a cold displeasure. “The glove. A loose end. And the man with the carriage. Another one. We have less time than I thought. The net is closing, not on me, but on this house. On you.” The dressing gown materialized in the doorway to the hall. “We go to Iping, Kemp. We go now. Get your coat. And prepare your dogcart. The Reign of Terror can wait. First, we must secure the means of our survival.” Kemp pushed himself off the door. He looked at the scarlet robe, the upright and strutting garment that contained a monster. He had passed the test. He had lied for him. He had become his shield. And his reward was to be sent on a desperate mission, a race against the law, to retrieve the very tools of his own enslavement. There was no escape. He was Griffin’s man now. He walked past the disembodied voice and the haunted robe, towards the front of the house to fetch his coat, his every step an act of surrender. The work was indeed just beginning.
